BOTTOM LINE. The paper is real, is in a top-3 journal, and its core quarterly association is more robust than I expected. But the two things the article actually wants to lean on — the 29% cumulative figure and the top-10-led size gradient — are the two least-vetted, least-identified objects in the paper. The 29% in particular fails on four independent grounds and must not carry weight. Full findings below, organized by attack surface.

=== 1. IDENTIFICATION: there is none, and the paper never claims otherwise until it does ===
Table 6.2 is a contemporaneous OLS time-series regression: quarterly excess return of the top-N portfolio over the S&P500, regressed on the same quarter's change in S&P500 index-fund ownership share. No instrument, no event study, no discontinuity, no difference-in-differences. I grepped the entire manuscript: the words "endogeneity," "reverse causality," "instrument," and "identification strategy" appear NOWHERE in the empirical section (the only hits for "identify"/"exogenous" are in the theory's algebra and one appendix sentence). The regression body correctly uses associational language throughout ("is associated with"). Then on p.36 the paper switches registers without warrant: "the rise in passive investing over the past 25 years CAUSED a firm that was in the top 50 ... to rise by 29% more than the index." That causal verb is not earned by anything in Section 6.

Reverse causality is not hypothetical here. PassiveFlow is net dollar flow into SPY/IVV/VOO + ICI S&P500 index mutual funds, scaled by index cap. Index-fund and ETF net flows are strongly performance-chasing at quarterly frequency. Controls include the contemporaneous and lagged S&P500 return, which absorbs the linear level-chasing channel — but the object at risk is precisely the nonlinear one: megacap-led rallies are the salient, headline-generating rallies that pull retail and 401(k) money into index products. A linear R_SP500 control cannot absorb "flows respond more strongly when the rally is led by the largest names," which is exactly the confound that would generate this coefficient with zero price impact.

DECISIVE TEST THE PAPER DECLINES TO RUN: there is no lagged-flow → return regression anywhere in the paper or its appendices. Not one. This is a two-line Stata change on a dataset they already have, and it is the natural test of whether flows PRECEDE the relative price move. Its absence is conspicuous. And note what happens in the one specification where they DO impose temporal ordering (Table 6.3, idiosyncratic volatility on one-quarter-lagged flow): the direct effect of lagged PassiveFlow is 20.63 with t = 1.21 — insignificant. Only the Top50 interaction survives (19.32, t = 2.53). So the single place in the paper where flows are dated before outcomes, the main effect vanishes.

=== 2. THE 29% IS ARITHMETIC, NOT AN ESTIMATE — and it is the article's weakest available number ===
The construction (p.36) is 0.528% × (0.05/0.09) × 99 = 29.04%. Algebraically this is just β_raw × cumulative flow, i.e. 5.87% of relative outperformance per 1 percentage point of index-fund ownership share, applied to the 4.95pp cumulative share increase. Four separate failures:

(a) FREQUENCY MISMATCH — the fatal one. The coefficient is identified off quarter-to-quarter deviations in the flow series (SD 0.09pp). The 29% applies that coefficient to the series' DRIFT term (mean 0.05pp/qtr), cumulated 99 times. These are different sources of variation. The regression contains no information about the low-frequency trend relationship; that variation is soaked up by the constant. The extrapolation projects a high-frequency slope 55 standard deviations out of sample (4.95pp / 0.09pp = 55 SDs) with no functional-form evidence whatsoever. Over 1996–2020 both the passive share and megacap concentration trended upward; the 29% is, structurally, a trend-on-trend attribution dressed as a regression result.

(b) THE AUTHORS' OWN MODEL REJECTS IT. Their calibrated structural model (Tables 5.2–5.5) produces a top-group premium of 0% (pure active-to-passive switch, full index — Table 5.2) up to ~4% (Table 5.5, partial large-stock index with noise traders). The paper states this plainly on p.36 and offers two unquantified excuses (fewer truly active investors than calibrated; partial mean-reversion). So the paper contains an unresolved internal inconsistency of a factor of 7 to infinity between its reduced form and the structural model the same authors built and calibrated to match empirical moments. An article that cites 29% is citing the number the paper's own theory cannot generate.

(c) NO STANDARD ERROR IS EVER REPORTED ON IT, and mean-reversion — the authors' own stated caveat — is never estimated despite being trivially testable (regress k-quarter-ahead cumulative excess returns on flow). Propagating only the coefficient's sampling error (t = 3.66 ⇒ SE ≈ 0.144), the 95% CI on 29.04% is roughly [13.5%, 44.6%]. That understates true uncertainty badly, since extrapolation and mean-reversion risk are the dominant terms and are unquantified.

(d) IT IS AN ARTIFACT OF THE top-50 CUT. Running the same cumulation on the paper's other four portfolios: top-10 → 37.8% [7.7%, 67.9%]; top-100 → 16.7%; top-150 → 11.4%; top-200 → 8.0% [−1.6%, 17.5%], insignificant. The "cumulative effect of passive on megacaps" therefore ranges from statistically zero to 68% depending on which arbitrary top-N line you draw. "29%" is not a finding; it is one point on a continuum, selected by reporting convention.

=== 3. VERSION DRIFT — the two load-bearing numbers are ~1 year old and were never seminar-tested ===
This is the finding I did not expect and it is important for the article's "best-credentialed" framing. I diffed three versions:
• NBER w28253 rev.1, Sept 2022 (Table 8): ONE large portfolio only (top 50, confirmed via matching descriptives: mean −0.15/−0.17, SD 1.56/1.86). No top-10/100/150/200 gradient. No cumulative extrapolation — grep for "Cumulating"/"cumulative effect" returns nothing.
• LSE FMG DP868-revised, April 2024: same. Still no gradient table, still no 29%.
• RFS accepted version, June 2025: Panel B (the five-portfolio monotone gradient, top-10 = 0.687%) and the 29% cumulation both appear for the first time.
Both therefore entered between April 2024 and June 2025, in the final RFS revision round(s), on a dataset frozen at 2020Q4. The paper's extensive vetting record — AFA, CICF, FIRS, Q-Group, Adam Smith Asset Pricing, BIS, LSE, and roughly a dozen seminars listed in the acknowledgments — is vetting of versions that did NOT contain either number. The credentialing the article is implicitly invoking does not extend to the specific figures it wants to quote.
Credit where due, and this matters: the top-50 quarterly coefficient is remarkably stable across the three versions (0.00549/0.00550/0.00523/0.00525 in 2022 and 2024 → 0.00557/0.00553/0.00531/0.00528 in 2025). That number has a genuine track record. The gradient and the 29% do not.

=== 4. SAMPLE AND WINDOW — the Mag-7 era is entirely out of sample ===
1996Q2–2020Q4, N = 99 quarterly aggregate observations. The sample end date is identical in the December 2020 first draft and the June 2025 accepted version: across 4.5 years of revision, roughly 18 additional quarters became available and none were added. Those 18 quarters (2021Q1–2025Q1) are precisely the period of the concentration surge the article wants to explain. "Magnificent Seven" is a 2023 coinage. The paper's in-sample concentration episodes are the dot-com run-up and the 2015–2020 FAANG run; it contains zero observations of the 2023–2025 concentration peak. I have no evidence the result would fail out of sample — but the article cannot represent this paper as evidence ABOUT the Mag 7. It is evidence about an earlier era, offered as a mechanism that might extend.
Additional sample concerns: the regressor has excess kurtosis 3.62 on N = 99, so a handful of quarters (plausibly 2000Q1, 2008Q4, 2020Q1–Q2) likely dominate the fit. No winsorization, no influence diagnostics, no robust regression, no bootstrap — I grepped for all of these and found none. There is also NO subsample or subperiod split anywhere in the paper (no "subsample," "subperiod," "first half," "second half," or dot-com-exclusion test). For a 25-year time-series regression with 99 observations spanning two structurally different concentration regimes, the absence of any temporal stability check is a standard referee demand that appears not to have been made.

=== 5. INFERENCE — the gradient is asserted, never tested; R² is thin ===
Adjusted R² across Table 6.2 Panel B: 0.049 (top-10), 0.125, 0.105, 0.124, 0.125. SEs are Newey-West with 3 lags on 99 observations.
The headline top-10 column is the WEAKEST cell in the table on every dimension except point estimate: largest coefficient (0.687), lowest t (2.46), lowest adjusted R² (0.049), and the noisiest dependent variable (top-10 excess return SD = 3.86% quarterly vs 1.86% for top-50). That is the signature of a small, lumpy portfolio — over 1996–2020 the top 10 is a handful of names whose relative return is driven by a few firm-specific episodes. The top-200 endpoint is insignificant (0.145, t = 1.64, p ≈ 0.10 two-sided).
Critically: the paper NEVER TESTS THE GRADIENT. There is no reported test that β_top10 > β_top200, no interaction specification, no joint test of monotonicity. The "monotone decline" is read off five point estimates whose confidence intervals overlap heavily (top-10 CI [0.140, 1.234]; top-200 CI [−0.028, 0.318]). A naive difference test assuming independence gives t ≈ 1.85 (p ≈ 0.06); the true SE is smaller than that because the portfolios are nested and positively correlated, so the gradient is probably real — but "probably real, never tested" is not the same as "established," and the article should not describe monotonicity as a finding of the paper when the paper never estimated it.
Multiple testing: five overlapping portfolios × {value-, equal-weighted} × {with, without controls}, plus S&P600, plus three concentration measures, plus idio-vol, plus month-start, plus idiosyncratic beta. No multiplicity adjustment anywhere. The nesting means these are not independent tests, but it also means the reported headline (top-50) is the strongest-t cell of a family.

=== 6. CONSTRUCT VALIDITY — the measure is narrow, and its meaning drifts within the sample ===
PassiveFlow covers only S&P500-tracking index mutual funds (ICI) plus three ETFs (SPY, IVV, VOO). Cumulative change over 25 years: 4.95pp of index capitalization. Excluded: total-market and broad-index funds, Russell/CRSP trackers, target-date funds, institutional internal indexation, and closet indexing — all of which also buy megacaps proportionally, and the paper's own introduction concedes passive growth is "more than twice as high" once benchmark-hugging is counted.
The paper discloses (p.32) that S&P500 index mutual funds are "47% to 87% of the assets of all index mutual funds invested in US stocks in our sample." That range is a within-sample drift: the regressor covers most of index investing early and roughly half of it late. So the omitted passive complex is (i) growing, (ii) positively correlated with the included regressor, and (iii) in the error term. That is time-varying measurement error in the construct; Newey-West does not touch it.
This produces a REDUCTIO that the article should confront directly. If the linear cumulation is valid, then applying the same 5.87%-per-pp multiplier to the broader passive share the article actually cares about (the paper's own stated ~16% of the market, or ~20pp of growth) yields cumulative megacap outperformance north of 100%. That is absurd, which means the linearity assumption underlying the 29% is self-refuting at exactly the scope the article wants to use it. Conversely, if only the narrow S&P500-fund slice has this effect, then the mechanism does not generalize to "passive inflates the Mag 7." The article cannot have it both ways.
Separately on the multiplier: β_raw implies ~5.9% relative price impact per 1pp of ownership share, PERMANENTLY, on a CROSS-SECTIONAL (relative) price. Aggregate-market inelasticity multipliers in the Gabaix–Koijen tradition are of similar order, but relative prices within the S&P500 should be far MORE elastic than the aggregate, because relative-value arbitrage within a large-cap index is cheap, unlevered, and unconstrained compared with levering the whole market. A relative-price multiplier as large as the aggregate one is theoretically uncomfortable and the paper does not address it.

=== 7. THE ROBUSTNESS TESTS ARE NOT INDEPENDENT ===
The paper calls two appendix exercises corroboration of Table 6.2. Neither is.
(a) Table E.8 (concentration): same 99 quarters, same regressor, and a dependent variable — change in the log combined index weight of the top 10 firms — that is very nearly an algebraic transform of the top-10 excess return already in Table 6.2 Panel B (for a fixed constituent set, Δlog w_top10 ≈ log((1+r_top10)/(1+r_index))). This is a restatement, not a replication. Its t-stats without controls are also marginal: 2.30, 2.02, 1.92 (the HHI version is below 2).
(b) Table E.9 (month-start dummy): described as "a proxy to capture exogenous variation," it is never used as an instrument for PassiveFlow, so it contributes nothing to the 0.687/0.528 estimates. And it is confounded by the turn-of-the-month return effect — documented since Ariel (JFE 1987), Lakonishok & Smidt (RFS 1988), and Ogden (JF 1990) — a calendar anomaly that long predates meaningful index-fund flows and has at least four competing explanations (paycheck/pension flows, month-end window dressing, cash-flow settlement timing, clustered information release). The paper cannot separate its interpretation from those. Notably, this test's own gradient also dies early: t = 2.28 (top-10), 2.82, 2.10, then 1.07 (top-150) and 0.16 (top-200), on adjusted R² of 0.0066 across 2.97M daily observations.

=== 8. THE PLACEBO IS WEAK, AND ITS POINT ESTIMATE HAS THE WRONG SIGN ===
Table 6.4 (S&P600, N = 77): coefficients are −0.0054, −0.0054, −0.0040, −0.0039, all insignificant (t = −1.26 to −0.75). The paper reports this as "consistent with our model," invoking the auxiliary prediction that flows lift an index's largest members only when those are also the economy's largest. Two problems. First, the point estimates are NEGATIVE and of roughly the same absolute magnitude as the S&P500 top-50 effect — the placebo is not a null, it is a mirror image, which is what one would expect if the S&P500 result were partly a size/style factor rather than a flow effect. Second, power: the S&P600 top-60 excess return has SD 3.41–3.89% (vs 1.86% for S&P500 top-50) on 77 rather than 99 observations, so implied SEs are ~0.42–0.43. The specification can only marginally reject the S&P500 magnitude (+0.528 sits ~2.2–2.5 SE from the S&P600 point estimates). More fundamentally, the model's flexibility means the S&P600 result cannot discipline the S&P500 result: the theory accommodates a positive, null, or negative coefficient depending on which index is tested, so no S&P600 outcome would have falsified anything.

=== 9. AUTHOR INCENTIVES — disclosed, mild, worth one clause ===
The paper acknowledges financial support from the LSE Paul Woolley Centre. Vayanos directs that centre, whose formal name is the Paul Woolley Centre for the Study of Capital Market Dysfunctionality — an institution founded on the thesis that delegated and benchmarked investment management causes market dysfunction. The paper also cites Vayanos & Woolley (2013) as theoretical support for the month-start test. This is academic, disclosed, and not industry money, so I weight it lightly: it is a research-program prior, not a financial conflict, and it does not by itself discount any coefficient. It is relevant only because the article proposes to present the paper as neutral best-available evidence; a one-clause disclosure is proportionate. There is a strong counterweight in the authors' favor: they voluntarily flag their own 29%-vs-4% discrepancy on the same page they report it, which is exactly what good-faith reporting looks like. The integrity problem here is downstream — an article that quotes 29% WITHOUT the caveat the authors themselves attached misrepresents the paper more than the paper misrepresents itself.

=== WHAT SURVIVES ===
One thing, cleanly: over 1996Q2–2020Q4, quarters with higher net flows into S&P500 index funds were quarters in which the index's largest constituents outperformed the index, ~+0.5%/quarter per one-SD flow for the top 50, t ≈ 3.7, adjusted R² ~0.13, stable to three decimals across three paper versions spanning 2022–2025. That is a robust contemporaneous ASSOCIATION over a window ending in 2020. Everything the article wants beyond that — the causal verb, the megacap-tilted gradient, the 29%, and the extension to the Mag 7 — is either untested, unidentified, out of sample, or contradicted by the paper's own calibration.

Audited against the published PDF (https://www.alexchinco.com/double-what-you-think-it-is.pdf, dated April 7 2024, downloaded and text-extracted locally to /private/tmp/claude-502/-Users-cissychen-design/0f8bdcde-3464-42f4-af17-1552808c31d6/scratchpad/cs_jfe.txt) and against the July 2022 working-paper version (https://foster.uw.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/1b-Sammon-Chinco-new-title.pdf, extracted to .../scratchpad/cs_2022.txt).

Bottom line: this is competent, transparently reported work with a public replication package (Mendeley x4vzjxkhtv). Its QUALITATIVE finding — that a material amount of index-tracking money sits outside the 40-Act fund universe — survives. Its 33.5% POINT ESTIMATE does not survive as a load-bearing central measurement. Nine specific defects, in descending severity.

=== 1. THE HEADLINE IS THE LOOSEST MEMBER OF ITS OWN PROXY FAMILY, AND THE TIGHTEST MEMBER FALSIFIES THE ARTICLE'S CLAIM ===
Table 4 (p.24) reports 2021 estimates across five proxies for "passive rebalancing volume": DailyVolume 33.50 (SE 2.91); DailyVolume−ADV 28.65 (2.91); Volume1600to2359 24.62 (2.70); VolumeAtClosingPrice 22.53 (2.10); VolumeAtClose 13.31 (1.96). The headline is column (1), the single most permissive definition — all volume on reconstitution day, with no subtraction of the stock's own normal trading.
The implied multiple vs the ICI's 16% therefore runs 0.83× → 1.54× → 1.79× → 2.09× → (2.41× with the Vanguard/CRSP add-on). The article's framing ("far above the fund-based number") is true under column (1), roughly half-true under column (3), and FALSE under column (5). The authors concede this in print (p.24–25): "there is no statistically measurable difference between our point estimate for %Indexed(2021) based on VolumeAtClose, 13.31% ± (1.96%), and ICI's estimate based on index-fund holdings, 16%." The point estimate under the most conservative proxy is BELOW the fund-based number.
Crucially, the paper elsewhere (p.14) names Volume1600to2359 as "our preferred intraday measure of passive rebalancing volume" — 24.62%, not 33.50%. The headline exceeds the authors' own stated preferred measure. A finding whose direction and magnitude are determined by an unforced definitional choice cannot anchor a section.

=== 2. ~27% OF THE HEADLINE HAS NO IDENTIFYING ARGUMENT BEHIND IT ===
The entire identification rests on one mechanism, laid out in §3.2 and Appendix D: passive rebalancing is prearranged (MOC orders, upstairs blocks, custom ETF redemption baskets via APs) and therefore prints at 4:00pm or in the minutes after. Appendix D's Dish Network worked example explicitly concludes "the only recorded trades got executed at market close." That argument, taken at face value, justifies at most Volume1600to2359 = 24.62%.
The gap 33.50 − 24.62 = 8.88pp — 27% of the headline — is INTRADAY volume on reconstitution day, precisely the volume the paper's own mechanism says passive investors do not generate. The defense offered (p.22) is negative and non-quantitative: the data are "not consistent with active investors delaying trades," and Admati–Pfleiderer sunshine trading "would not apply." That is an argument, not a measurement. Column (2) shows that merely subtracting the stock's own ADV — the weakest conceivable contamination adjustment — removes 4.85pp, and the authors themselves concede this "suggests that our headline numbers might be overestimating the true passive ownership share by somewhere between 2%pt and 5%pt." Reconstitution day is a high-news, high-liquidity, index-arbitrage-unwind day; active/arb volume is plausibly a multiple of ADV, not one ADV.

=== 3. THREE OF FIVE INDEXES — 65% OF THE HEADLINE — RECONSTITUTE ON TRIPLE-WITCHING DAYS, THE EXACT CONTAMINATION THE AUTHORS' OWN EARLIER DRAFT USED AS AN EXCLUSION CRITERION ===
Published paper, p.9: "S&P Dow Jones regularly reconstitutes the S&P 500 and MidCap 400 on a quarterly basis. These scheduled events take place on the third Friday of March, June, September, and December which represent triple-witching days." p.10–11 on the Nasdaq 100: "This annual rebalancing event lines up with the final witching day of the calendar year."
The 2022 working paper (cs_2022.txt, p.9–10) explicitly excluded such indexes for this reason: "on these days, there is high closing volume for reasons unrelated to any reconstitution events. This limits the number of benchmark indexes we can use in our analysis. Many indexes, such as the Nasdaq 100, always reconstitute on triple-witching days… if we were to include these indexes in our analysis, we would tend to overstate the passive-ownership share. And we are trying to be as conservative as possible."
The published version reinstates all three. From Table 3 (2021): S&P 500 16.80 + S&P MidCap 400 1.12 + Nasdaq 100 3.76 = 21.68pp of the 33.50pp headline (65%) comes from witching-contaminated indexes. The only defense in the published text is an unquantified assertion that scheduled and ad hoc changes yield "similar point estimates" — no table, no test. The two clean, non-witching, direct-weight indexes (Russell 1000 + 2000) contribute 11.83pp. The authors reversed a stated exclusion rule in the direction of a larger number and did not show the reversal is harmless.

=== 4. VERSION DRIFT IS FAR WORSE THAN A 37.8→33.5 RENUMBERING; THE METHOD UNDERNEATH THE NUMBER WAS REPLACED ===
2022 version: 37.8% for 2020, THREE indexes (S&P 500, Russell 1000/2000), sample 2011–2021 (Russell 2011–2020), estimator = RebalVolume_n / #Tradable_n × IndexCap with explicit FLOAT ADJUSTMENT, proxy = VolumeAtClose defined as 4:00–4:20pm, framed as a LOWER BOUND ("37.8% is a lower bound… almost certainly too low").
2024 published: 33.5% for 2021, FIVE indexes, sample 2000–2021, estimator = DailyVolume × Price / IndexWeight (eq. 4), NO float adjustment for four of five indexes, proxy = all-day volume, framed as a point estimate inside a range.
The decisive comparison: the SAME construct that produced 37.8% in 2022 (closing volume) produces 11.54% for 2020 in the published Table 4, column (5). The headline magnitude survived across versions only because the volume window was widened from ~20 minutes to a full trading day and the normalizer was swapped. The epistemic label also flipped from "lower bound" to point estimate. This is textbook specification drift: the conclusion was stable while the method that generated it was not. Nothing in the published paper reconciles the two versions.

=== 5. CONSTRUCT VALIDITY: THE SERIES DOES NOT BEHAVE LIKE AN OWNERSHIP STOCK ===
Table 3 totals: 2007 16.33 → 2008 25.31 → 2009 31.85 → 2010 24.32 → 2013 23.21 → 2021 33.50. A share of the market owned by passive investors cannot rise 15.5pp in two years, fall 8.6pp in the next four, and do so while the observable component (index-fund ownership) rose monotonically throughout. What the series tracks is reconstitution-day trading intensity, which spikes with volatility and liquidity-provision activity. The authors acknowledge the anomaly and route around it: Appendix B fits a Kalman filter that imposes a constant index-fund-to-passive ratio, notes the filtered series shows "no spike in ownership following the 2008 financial crises," and calls this "expected." They do not take the implication — that if the 2009 spike is spurious, the same contaminant is present at every point in the series, including 2021.
Related: the Nasdaq 100 component runs 0.64 (2014) → 1.17 (2018) → 3.76 (2021), a 6× move on the smallest event count in the sample (Figure 3: mean 23 changes/yr, min 12). Nasdaq 100 alone supplies 2.59pp of the 4.07pp increase in the headline from 2018 to 2021 — 64% of the recent growth comes from the least reliable index in the set (witching-day reconstitution, third-party Siblis quarterly weights interpolated to daily, no float adjustment, and CRSP market-cap weights used as a proxy for a MODIFIED/capped-weight index whose true weights differ from cap weights by construction).

=== 6. REPORTED STANDARD ERRORS MEASURE THE WRONG THING AND CONVEY FALSE PRECISION ===
The SEs (33.50 ± 2.91) are clustered by announcement and are, by the paper's own decomposition (§2.4), ~80% within-event dispersion: how much implied-AUM varies across the ~1,156 add/drop events in a year. They quantify sampling noise CONDITIONAL on the identifying assumption that reconstitution-day volume is passive rebalancing. They carry zero information about the bias from that assumption. The proxy family spread (13.31 → 33.50, ~20pp) is roughly 7× the reported SE. Any use of "33.5% ± 2.9%" implies a precision the design cannot deliver.
Multiple-comparison exposure compounds this: 5 proxies × 5 indexes × 22 years, with the headline taken as the maximum proxy in the terminal year.

=== 7. THE ESTIMATOR IS 1/w AND THE AUTHORS' OWN DIAGNOSTIC SHOWS THE SIGNATURE OF ADDITIVE CONTAMINATION ===
Eq. (4): implied AUM = DollarVolume / IndexWeight. Average index weights are tiny (Table 1a: S&P 500 adds 9.4 bps; Russell 1000 direct adds 4.5 bps; Russell 2000 direct adds 2.4 bps), so any error in w is amplified non-linearly, and eq. (5) takes an ARITHMETIC MEAN of these ratios rather than a value-weighted aggregate — a heavy-right-tail object.
Table 6 column (4) regresses %Error on IndexWeight and finds −0.01 with t = 4.46. The authors read this as "we underestimate for large-weight stocks." The mechanically equivalent and more parsimonious reading is the reverse: if reconstitution-day volume = w × AUM_passive + V_active, then implied AUM = AUM_passive + V_active/w, which rises exactly as w falls. Their own regression is the fingerprint of an additive non-passive volume component. They do not test this alternative. Column (3) ($Volume, +0.19) points the same way. Together these are the two coefficients most diagnostic of contamination, and neither is engaged with.

=== 8. INPUT-DATA QUALITY IS WEAKEST WHERE THE ESTIMATE IS LARGEST ===
The paper states plainly (p.28): "most of our measurement error seems to be coming from uncertainty about the precise weights used by the indexes… Our measurement error all but disappears when we have precise index weights directly from the index provider." Direct daily weights exist only for the Russell 1000/2000 from 2009 (purchased from FTSE Russell for $7,500). Everything else is interpolated from quarterly observations: S&P 500 (S&P DJI quarterly, float-adjusted), S&P MidCap 400 (Siblis, NOT float-adjusted), Nasdaq 100 (Siblis, NOT float-adjusted), Russell pre-2009 (NOT float-adjusted).
Table 5 average absolute measurement error per event: S&P 500 ±5.49pp, Russell 1000 ±1.87, Nasdaq 100 ±0.74, S&P MidCap ±0.35, Russell 2000 ±0.23. The S&P 500 — which supplies 16.80pp, half the headline — has per-event error 3–24× worse than every other index. The internal consistency condition the authors themselves impose (eq. 8: the add-implied and drop-implied AUM must agree) fails most badly precisely on the component that matters most.

=== 9. THE PAPER'S OWN LIKE-FOR-LIKE RECONCILIATION IMPLIES A SHADOW-PASSIVE MULTIPLE OF 5–8×, NOT 2× ===
This is the quietest and most damaging item. Intro p.4 and Appendix B: "if all passive investing was index-fund investing, we would have estimated a value of around 6% not 16%," derived from the Table B2 panel (b) slope of 0.16 on the five-index row (0.16 × 33.5 ≈ 6). Note the derivation itself is loose — it uses a slope as if it were a level, and the fitted line with its −1.17 intercept actually gives −1.17 + 0.16×33.5 = 4.19%.
So the internally consistent comparison is 33.5% (five indexes, volume-implied) vs 4.2–6% (same five indexes, holdings-observed index funds) — a shadow-passive multiple of 5.6× to 8×, meaning 82–87% of the number is unobserved residual carried entirely by the untested identifying assumption. The "double" headline is manufactured by comparing a five-index numerator against an all-index denominator. Both directions of the mismatch are acknowledged by the authors in passing ("The ICI's 16% figure is not a lower bound because it is based on more indexes"), but the title, abstract and every downstream citation use the 2× framing.
For calibration, the closest independent holdings-based anchor the paper itself cites — BlackRock's 2017 white paper (Novick et al.), $5.0t index funds vs $6.8t internal indexers — implies a shadow-passive multiple of ~1.4×. The paper's implicit 5.6–8× is an extraordinary claim that the paper never states as such and never defends.

=== INCENTIVES / COI ===
No material COI found. Both authors are academics (Chinco, Baruch Zicklin; Sammon, HBS Finance); no industry funding disclosed; replication package is public. Two soft points only: (a) the title "Double What You Think It Is" is a salience choice that locks in the column-(1) proxy, and (b) the acknowledgments include industry practitioners with a stake in the size of the passive-rebalancing complex (Vanguard's Rodney Comegys, Norges Bank Index Management presentation, index-industry researchers) — normal in this literature and not disqualifying. Sammon remains at HBS as of 2026 with active working papers on direct indexing and leveraged ETFs; no revision or retraction of the estimate has been issued.

=== EXTERNAL SCRUTINY: THIN ===
Two years post-publication I found no published replication, no comment paper, and no formal critique of the reconstitution-volume estimator. Regulators and practitioners cite the 33.5% uncritically as a point estimate — the FCA occasional paper in the local corpus (.../scratchpad/v32/fca_new.txt, lines 833, 1298, 1313) restates it flatly, then in the very next paragraph describes the arbitrageur pre-positioning/unwind mechanism that contaminates the estimator, without connecting the two. The only substantive published objection I located is non-academic: Joachim Klement (Klement on Investing) argues the design "conflates active and passive investor behavior" because active managers also concentrate trades at the close for liquidity, and because mandate constraints force active funds to trade index adds/drops on exactly these dates — "there is no way the data used in the study above is able to distinguish between these active and passive investors." That is the same objection as item 2, arrived at independently.
Absence of critique is not corroboration. A single-team, single-method estimate that no one has re-run is exactly the profile that should not be load-bearing.

The estimate is for 2021; the sample ends there. Given item 5 the series is not stable enough to extrapolate five years forward. Any naive extension of the estimator past 2025 is invalid without re-derivation. An article written in August 2026 must not present 33.5% as a current figure.

## 0. What I audited against
INFORMS blocked direct fetch (403). ## 1. IDENTIFICATION — the IV is largely NOT causally identified. This is the finding that drives my verdict.

The IV specification (Eqs. 5–6, p. 27) uses **two excluded instruments**:
- `Post` — an indicator for the ±3-year window *after* the index event, **switched on for treated AND control firms alike**
- `Post × Treated × PassiveGap` — the genuine difference-in-differences instrument

Second stage: `Outcome = α + β₃·P̂assive + FE + ε`. **Fixed effects are firm-by-cohort ONLY. There are no calendar-time fixed effects anywhere in the IV.** (Confirmed by grep: `time fixed effects` appears only in the OLS sections, lines 707, 1672, 1697, 2964.)

`Post` is therefore a pure pre/post *calendar-time* contrast, common to treated and control firms, in a panel where **both** the endogenous regressor (passive ownership, rising monotonically 1990→2019, Fig. 1) **and** the outcome (|Ret|/SD rising 1.0→3.5, Fig. 1) trend strongly upward. Its Wald ratio is nothing but (secular drift in outcome)/(secular drift in passive ownership). That is precisely the aggregate correlation the OLS's year-quarter FE were built to purge.

**I decomposed the 2SLS into instrument-specific Wald ratios using the paper's own printed coefficients (Table 3, p. 29; reduced form Table D3, p. 59):**

| Spec | Wald(`Post`) | Wald(DiD) | Reported 2SLS |
|---|---|---|---|
| Russell \|Ret\| | 0.175* | 0.102 | **0.160** |
| Russell \|Ret\|/SD | 15.50 | 0.91 | **11.68** |
| Russell PJ | 1.50 | **−0.175** | **0.90** |
| Russell IVD | 0.50 | 0.525 | **0.36** |
| S&P \|Ret\| | 0.222 | 0.089 | **0.221** |
| S&P \|Ret\|/SD | 15.44 | 2.55 | **14.74** |
| S&P PJ | 1.78 | 1.31 | **1.57** |
| S&P IVD | 0.556 | **−0.233** | **0.413** |

(*Russell |Ret| `Post` RF prints as "0.00***" at 2dp; imputed ≈0.0035 from the S&P panel's 0.004. Every other cell uses printed coefficients. Samples differ trivially between tables — S&P N=263,348 vs 262,893.)

**In 7 of 8 specifications the reported 2SLS sits essentially on the `Post` Wald ratio and far from the DiD Wald ratio. For S&P |Ret| the match is exact to three digits (0.221 vs 0.222).** With 2SLS the estimate is a first-stage-variance-weighted combination of instrument-specific Walds; `Post` has a first-stage t of ~18–20 and varies across the whole sample, while the DiD instrument is nonzero only for treated firms and is scaled by `PassiveGap` (≈0.01–0.03), so it receives almost no weight. The numbers confirm this exactly.

**Consequences:**
1. The "causal" upgrade the article relies on is, arithmetically, a time-series ratio of two trends, not a difference-in-differences.
2. The `Post` instrument's exclusion restriction is transparently false. Over 1990–2019 the pre/post windows straddle Reg FD (Aug 2000), decimalization (2001), intensified insider-trading enforcement (Coffee 2007 — Sammon himself names it, p. 14), Sarbanes-Oxley (2002), the 2004 expansion of Form 8-K, Reg NMS (2007), and the rise of algorithmic trading. **Sammon's Reg FD check (Table C1 cols 9–12, 2001–2019 subsample) and his AT check (MIDAS controls, 2012+) are applied ONLY to the OLS. Neither is ever applied to the IV.**
3. **This resolves — against the author — the paper's own headline reassurance.** Sammon argues (p. 27) that IV > OLS by 2.5–4× proves the OLS is not biased by reverse causality. The real explanation is mundane: the OLS has year-quarter FE and the IV does not. The IV/OLS gap measures how much of the IV comes from the trend.
4. **The reduced form is the Anderson–Rubin test.** On the only instrument with a defensible exclusion restriction, the paper's own Table D3 gives: **7 of 8 coefficients statistically insignificant, and 2 of 8 with the WRONG SIGN** (Russell PJ −0.31; S&P IVD −0.138). AR inference is fully robust to weak instruments; a first-stage F of 222 does not rescue it, because that F is driven by `Post`. Sammon's defense (Appendix D.5) invokes Lochner–Moretti and Chernozhukov–Hansen to argue an IV t-stat can exceed a reduced-form t-stat in finite samples, plus a shadow-indexing story. **That defense addresses magnitude of t-stats; it does not address wrong-signed reduced forms, and it never confronts the `Post` instrument.**
5. **The author knew.** March 2023 draft, footnote 21: *"Because I am using both Post and Post×Treated×PassiveGap as instruments for passive ownership, the time trend and the change in passive ownership associated with being treated are jointly driving the large magnitude of the F-statistic."* **This footnote is absent from the Oct 2023 / published version** (grep for "jointly" returns nothing). Disclosure of a known weakness regressed between drafts.
6. No overidentification test (Hansen J / Sargan) is reported despite 2 instruments for 1 endogenous regressor. Given the two Wald ratios differ by up to 17×, a J test would almost certainly reject.
7. The Heath–Ringgenberg–Samadi–Werner "reused natural experiments" defense (p. 32: "almost all my IV t-statistics are over 3.62") **collapses with the IV**, since those t-stats come from the contaminated instrument. The DiD-identified t-stats are ~0.2–1.5 and fail any reuse-adjusted threshold.

## 3. CONSTRUCT VALIDITY — the measures cannot separate "less anticipation" from "more news at the announcement," and the paper never engages the literature that says it's the latter

Every measure is built on the same numerator, the earnings-day absolute market-adjusted return. The identifying assumption is that the *total* information in an announcement is held fixed, so a bigger jump means less was anticipated. That assumption is stated but never tested.

**Beaver, McNichols & Wang, "The information content of earnings announcements," Review of Accounting Studies 23(1):95–135 (2018)**, and **Beaver, McNichols & Wang, "Increased market response to earnings announcements in the 21st century," Journal of Accounting and Economics 69(1) (2020)**, document a *dramatic increase in the information content of earnings announcements from 2001 onward* — attributed to more information being conveyed *at* the announcement (bundled guidance, richer press releases, conference calls, expanded 8-K disclosure), not to reduced anticipation. That is the same trend, in the same window, with the same numerator, and the opposite interpretation. **Sammon's paper cites neither: grep for "Beaver" returns zero hits across the full text.** Sammon's own text notes his |Ret|/SD trend "accelerates around 2001" (p. 14) — exactly Beaver et al.'s inflection point — and attributes it to Reg FD and insider-trading enforcement without considering the disclosure-content channel.

PJ is not immune: it is the post-announcement share of |pre| + |post| cumulative return, so it rises mechanically when the announcement-window numerator grows.

Two pieces of **the paper's own evidence** point at the alternative:
- **Table D5 col. 3**: |SUE|/P is significantly *higher* for high-passive stocks (0.00874**). Sammon reads this as "analysts became less accurate." It is equally consistent with "these firms' announcements carry more news." (Note also a text/table discrepancy: the text calls col. 4 "positive and statistically insignificant" while the table prints 2.119*** (0.446).)
- **Table D7**: firms added to the S&P 500 show an **increase in earnings volatility**. This is a direct exclusion-restriction violation for the S&P IV in the same direction as the result — bigger news, not less anticipation. Sammon dismisses it with a single anecdote about Tesla gaming regulatory credits to qualify for index inclusion. An anecdote is not a control.

The cross-sectional OLS is partially protected here: year-quarter FE absorb the *aggregate* rise in announcement content. The attack that survives is that high-passive firms (large, S&P 500, heavily covered) differentially expanded bundled disclosure. Sammon controls for size, B/M, age, momentum, beta, R², total and idiosyncratic vol, and total institutional ownership — **but for no disclosure-practice variable** (guidance issuance, conference-call presence, 8-K bundling). This is a live, unaddressed confound in the specification that produces the load-bearing number.

## 4. INFERENCE AND MULTIPLE COMPARISONS

- The headline "1/4th of the mean" is an **unweighted average of four hand-picked, highly collinear measures** (all functions of the same earnings-day return). It has **no standard error**. It is a presentational construct, not an estimated quantity.
- **The four measures are not the four the author started with.** March 2023 draft: outcomes were `QVS`, `DM`, `jump`. Published version: `|Ret|`, `|Ret|/SD`, `PJ` (=jump), `IVD`. **QVS and DM appear zero times in the Oct 2023 text.** Two primary outcomes were dropped and three new ones introduced between drafts. No multiple-testing adjustment is reported anywhere, and the effective specification search across drafts spans at least seven candidate measures.
- SEs are double-clustered at firm and year-quarter (OLS) / firm and quarter (IV) — appropriate. The 441,238-observation panel is ample. No complaint on power.
- The extrapolation "15% more passive ownership → X" is a linear projection of a within-quarter cross-sectional slope onto a 30-year aggregate change. The FE that make the coefficient credible are exactly the FE that make this extrapolation illegitimate: **the OLS is identified off within-firm, within-quarter variation and says nothing directly about a market-wide time trend.**

No financial conflict. Sammon is an academic (Associate Professor, HBS Finance; verified still at HBS as of 2026 — no industry affiliation found). No disclosed funding from asset managers or index providers. The relevant incentive is ordinary research-program commitment: Sammon's portfolio (Chinco & Sammon, *"The Passive-Ownership Share Is Double What You Think It Is"*, JFE 2024; Greenwood & Sammon on index inclusion) is built on passive-investing effects being large. ## 7. DATA CONSTRUCTION

Passive ownership = CRSP MF (index funds + all ETFs + name-matched) → MFLINKS → **Thomson S12 holdings**. **Schwarz & Potter show ~20% of SEC-reported mutual fund portfolios are missing from S12, and TR coverage deteriorates markedly post-2008** (Zhu, "The Missing New Funds": 58% of new U.S. equity share classes 2008–2015 unmatched to TR). ETFs — the fastest-growing passive vehicle and the majority of passive AUM by the end of the sample — are notoriously spotty in S12. Sammon's robustness (Appendix C.3, restricting to the CRSP "D" index flag) varies the *definition* of passive, not the *holdings source*, so it does not test this. Direction of bias is ambiguous (classical error attenuates β; understated Δ inflates the counterfactual), so I flag this as a magnitude-precision problem rather than a directional one — but it means the headline number carries more uncertainty than its stars suggest.

## 8. WHAT SURVIVES — why this is RESTRICTED_USE, not VETO

The cross-sectional OLS is a genuinely solid piece of work and I will not pretend otherwise: 441,238 observations, firm **and** year-quarter fixed effects, ten controls deliberately chosen to match the Glosten–Nallareddy–Zou characteristic set, SEs double-clustered on both dimensions, four measures all significant in the same direction (t ≈ 3.7–11.5), robust to value-weighting (shrinks but survives at 1%), robust to the post-Reg-FD 2001–2019 subsample, robust to Weller's algorithmic-trading controls, robust to a narrower passive definition, and peer-reviewed at Management Science. **"Within a given quarter, U.S. stocks with higher passive ownership have larger, less-anticipated earnings-day price moves"** is a defensible, replicable claim.

**But that is not the claim the article wants to make.** The article uses this paper as "the strongest evidence that SOME price-discovery channel measurably deteriorated." That framing leans on the paper's **two weakest components**: (a) the uncontrolled aggregate time trend in Figure 1 — descriptive, unadjusted, interpretively contested by Beaver–McNichols–Wang, and partially reversed after 2019 by Sammon's own Figure E.11; and (b) the causal IV, which my Wald decomposition shows is substantially identified by an invalid time-trend instrument. **There is an inversion here the article must not miss: the robust part of the paper is cross-sectional and does not speak to a market-wide deterioration; the part that speaks to market-wide deterioration is the part that is not robust.**

VETO would be wrong — the underlying association is real and published. But the number cannot carry the article's weight in its current form.

Greenwood & Sammon (Journal of Finance 80(2), 2025) measure how much prices respond to index-driven trading over an overlapping window with independent data and find the multiplier FELL by a factor of 7 to 20 (M: 6.75 in the late 1990s to 0.37 in 2010-2020 for additions; 10.76 to 0.7 for deletions), robust to migrations, front-running and controls. If the 11% appears, that finding must appear beside it.

If the article's sentence is 'passive changed how prices respond to trading,' the 11% is the WRONG evidence for it. HHL estimate a quarterly 13F demand slope; the price-response claim is what Greenwood-Sammon measures directly and rejects. Either restate the claim as 'the estimated slope of aggregate demand' (narrow, model-internal) or use it only alongside the contest.

State the level, not just the percentage. HHL's own translation: the price impact of buying $1 of a stock rises 'roughly from $2.5 to $2.8.' A 12% move in the dollar multiplier is not a regime change, and a reader who sees only '11% more inelastic' will infer one.

Do not cite Behmaram (2026) as independent corroboration. Same data (13F/FactSet), same Koijen-Yogo framework, and he runs HHL's own equation (29). If used, disclose that it is a within-paradigm extension AND that its counterfactual implies ~43% (elasticity 0.139 vs 0.245 frozen at 2000), roughly 4x HHL's 11% — so it corroborates the two-thirds-offset structure while contesting the headline number.

If the article states a number at all, prefer a RANGE with its source of variation: 6.3% on HHL's fund-based measure, 11% on their broad elasticity-defined measure, ~43% in Behmaram's stock-level counterfactual. A single point estimate misrepresents the state of the literature.

Do not write that passive investing drove the observed decline in measured elasticity. HHL's own realized series goes 0.41 to 0.27 but 'increase[s] until before the financial crisis, and ha[s] been decreasing since' — non-monotonic, while passive growth was monotonic. The 11% is a model counterfactual, not a fitted trend.

Note that the pass-through of 0.33 is itself contested: HHL concede in-text that Coles, Heath & Ringgenberg (JFE 2022) 'show a full degree of strategic substitution,' i.e. a pass-through near zero, from a different identification.

If citing HHL as unengaged-by-critics, verify against the AER-typeset version (AER 115(3), March 2025) — I confirmed the absence of Greenwood & Sammon only in the March 2024 working paper. Do not assert the omission without that check.

Do not source the number from Apollo Academy (von Moltke & Sløk, 2024) or other secondary coverage; it restates HHL with no added data and comes from a private-markets manager with a stake in the thesis.
